offered_action_specs.name: rollback_deploy
offered_action_specs.description: Roll one service back to the settings it ran before its latest deploy, as the deploy log records them. Code plans it from that log, not from your tools' results, so you can name it even when they cannot see deploys: if the log holds no deploy of that service to undo, or the service changed since, code refuses it. Its container is recreated, so the service pauses while it restarts. Money already booked wrong stays wrong: a rollback stops new damage, and repairs nothing.

proposed.why: The evidence points to the 11:04:10 payments-api deploy exhausting its Postgres connection pool, and a rollback is the fitting fix.

diagnosis.hypothesis: The payments-api deploy at 11:04:10 (settings shown: PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, REFUND_CONNECTION=kept) brought in a Postgres connection leak, most likely in the refund path that REFUND_CONNECTION controls. After the deploy, a refund at 11:04:25.013 still completed in 15 ms. From 11:04:25.4 on, every request that needs the database (POST /payments and refunds) waits about 5 s for a pool connection and fails with psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout (HTTP 500). That pins p95 latency near 5 to 7 s. The provider is not the cause: our calls to it stay at about 6 ms p95. Still open: I could not see the settings before the deploy, so I cannot prove that REFUND_CONNECTION is the setting that changed. That the refund path holds connections is an inference from the timing and from the setting's name, not something I watched happen. I did not run the money check.

evidence.shows: p95 of POST /payments was 0.02 to 0.04 s until 11:04:02, then 7.33 s at 11:05:02. The alert's symptom is confirmed.

payments-api was redeployed at 11:04:10Z with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept, PROVIDER_BREAKER=on and CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, about 20 s before the slow requests began. All other services date from 11:02:44.
payments-api's calls to the provider stay fast (about 5 to 9 ms p95) through the spike, so the provider is not the bottleneck.
The slow payments-api requests (POST /payments and refunds) all take almost exactly 5.0 s, starting at 11:04:26. That uniform duration points to a timeout.

A slow POST /payments trace spends about 5 s with no child span between a Redis SET and an EVAL, then ends with status 500 and error.type psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout. It was waiting for a database connection.
payments-api's error logs are full of PoolTimeout exceptions on POST /payments.

Before 11:04:10, refunds took 6 to 23 ms. After the deploy, one refund at 11:04:25.013 took 15 ms, and every refund from 11:04:25.4 on takes about 5 s. This fits connections being held after the new refund code path runs.

proposed_fix.summary: Roll payments-api back to the settings it ran before the 11:04:10 deploy, most likely restoring the earlier REFUND_CONNECTION behavior. Recreating the container also frees the leaked pool connections. After that, confirm that POST /payments p95 is back under 2 s and the PoolTimeout errors have stopped. Then run money_check, because payments and refunds that failed with 500 in the window may have left partial state.

diagnosis.blast_radius: payments-api pauses while its container is recreated, so in-flight payment and refund requests fail and clients must retry with their idempotency keys. The rollback also reverts PROVIDER_BREAKER and CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT if those changed in the same deploy. The rollback repairs nothing already booked wrong.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: If things get worse, redeploy payments-api with the 11:04:10 settings (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, REFUND_CONNECTION=kept), and investigate further with refunds rate-limited.
